🚨 99% of Python beginners learn the wrong way.
They jump between random YouTube videos... Watch 100 tutorials... Build nothing.
If I had to start Python again in 2026, this is the exact roadmap I'd follow👇
🐍 Python Master Cheatsheet (2026)
1. Basics
Learn variables, indentation, comments, input/output, and Python syntax. This is the foundation—skip it and everything else feels confusing.
2. Data Types
Understand integers, floats, strings, booleans, lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries. Every Python program is built on these.
3. Operators
Master arithmetic, comparison, logical, and assignment operators to perform calculations and make decisions.
4. Control Flow
Use if, elif, else, for, and while loops to control how your program behaves.
5. Functions
Write reusable code with def, parameters, return values, default arguments, and clean function design.
6. Strings
Manipulate text using slicing, formatting, .split(), .join(), .replace(), and f-strings.
7. Lists
Store collections of data. Learn indexing, slicing, appending, removing, sorting, and looping.
8. Tuples
Immutable collections that are faster and safer when your data shouldn't change.
9. Sets
Remove duplicates, perform unions/intersections, and speed up lookups.
10. Dictionaries
Store data as key-value pairs. Essential for APIs, JSON, and real-world applications.
11. List Comprehensions
Write cleaner and more Pythonic code in a single line.
12. Lambda Functions
Create small anonymous functions for sorting, filtering, and quick operations.
13. File Handling
Read, write, and manage files using open(), with, and file modes.
14. Exception Handling
Use try, except, finally, and raise so your programs don't crash unexpectedly.
15. Modules
Leverage Python's standard library (math, os, datetime, random) instead of reinventing the wheel.
16. Built-in Functions
Master len(), sum(), range(), sorted(), max(), min() and dozens more to write efficient code.
17. Pip
Install and manage packages like NumPy, Pandas, Requests, and Flask with ease.
18. Virtual Environments
Keep project dependencies isolated to avoid version conflicts.
19. Magic (Dunder) Methods
Learn __init__, __str__, __repr__, and more to write professional object-oriented Python.
20. Best Practices
Write readable code, follow PEP 8, use meaningful names, handle errors, and build projects consistently.
📌 Master these 20 topics, and you'll have a strong Python foundation for: • AI & Machine Learning • Data Science • Automation • Web Development • Backend APIs • Cybersecurity

Christopher Nolan gave Ludwig Göransson one instruction for The Odyssey: no orchestra. Not a stylistic preference, a flat ban. An instrument that didn’t exist in the Bronze Age couldn’t score a film set in it.
So Göransson had to build a musical language from instruments nobody alive has ever heard played correctly. The aulos, a double reed pipe carved into Greek pottery for a thousand years, has no surviving reeds. Musician Callum Armstrong spent weeks with two collaborators reading ancient source material just to work out how the mouthpiece functioned. The lyre, added at Nolan’s specific request to represent the pluck of Odysseus drawing his bow, was reconstructed the same way, performer Rosa Fragorapti describing the process as cross referencing iconography and philological sources against her own musicianship, because no continuous playing tradition survived to teach her directly.
Then Göransson added 35 bronze gongs sized to the Bronze Age setting, layered under synthesizers, and brought in James Blake for what he calls the score’s emotional pacing, a contemporary human voice inside a sonic world built entirely from instruments most audiences have never encountered.
None of this reads like a composer sprinkling in a historical flourish. It reads like archaeology performed in real time, a team reverse engineering how a civilization actually sounded from urns and carvings because the instruments and the people who knew how to play them are three thousand years gone. Göransson’s own line cuts through the research: the orchestra never existed back then, so the absence wasn’t a constraint to work around, it was the actual assignment.

A guy from the AI ​​industry showed me Seedance 2.0. It blew my mind.

This is the first model that takes multiple inputs at once — two images, two videos, and audio, all in a single generation. The model decides how to combine them based on your prompt.

Here's what that actually enables:

Swapping the character and background in a finished video — tag the references directly in the prompt, and what used to take a production studio weeks now takes 60 seconds.

Motion from the original video stays exact — just say "keep the same movement," and it preserves the camera and character choreography perfectly.

Virtual outfit try-on on real footage of a person — no distortion on the face at all. Even an AI expert couldn't tell it apart from real footage.

Translating an ad across languages while swapping the actor, in one prompt — every gesture and movement preserved, perfect for A/B testing across markets.

Extending video — take a 3-second clip, tell it what happens next, and the model builds out the scene while keeping the character consistent.

One interesting detail: the best prompt engineer for this model isn't a person — it's Claude. According to the tester, Claude (Opus 4.6) understands vision-model prompting better than any other LLM he's tried.

This isn't a video generator anymore. It's a next-generation video editor.

YouTube: "Greg Isenberg" - I tested Seedance 2.0. Wow.

I recommend everyone to watch this interview. It shows all the possibilities and life hacks. This free video gives more benefits than $500 courses

Our recent research on generative spatial reasoning: When you ask someone "Where is the cup?", they will usually point it out directly instead of stating "The target is enclosed within the bounding box [345, 512, 412, 600]".

Spatial ability inherently exists within continuous visual space, yet nearly all existing spatial tasks demand responses in the form of coordinates, multiple-choice selections or textual descriptions. This paradigm feels highly unnatural for VLMs and inevitably forces these models to resort to rote memorization. While text-to-image, video generation and world models are capable of rendering outputs visually, accurate evaluation and comparative analysis remain unachievable.

🛠️ To address this issue, we propose an agentic visual protocol framework that instructs generative models to directly "respond" on images via the most appropriate visual manners—including marking target objects, generating depth maps and drawing motion trajectories. Meanwhile, the framework autonomously builds parsers to convert these pixel-level visual answers into structured textual data, supporting standardized evaluation and comparative measurement of spatial capabilities between VLMs and generative models.

Show, Don't Tell: Evaluating Spatial Cognition in Generative Pixels Rather Than LLM Text
